blocks.html: Data communication is the exchange of data (text, images, audio, video) between two devices over a transmission medium. Sending a WhatsApp message, making a UPI payment, joining an online class and watching a YouTube video are all data communication.

blocks.html: Without a common protocol, the receiver would not understand what the sender means, just as two people who do not share a language cannot talk.

Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a channel can carry, measured in hertz (Hz). A wider bandwidth can carry more data, just as a wider road can carry more traffic. In everyday speech, people also use "bandwidth" to mean the speed of a connection.
The data transfer rate is the number of bits sent per second, measured in bits per second (bps).
(Networking normally uses these decimal steps of 1,000. Some textbooks use 1,024 instead; follow your board's convention in the exam.)
Bits vs bytes: speeds are given in bits (small b), and file sizes in bytes (capital B). 1 byte = 8 bits. A "100 Mbps" connection therefore downloads at most 100 / 8 = 12.5 MB per second.

blocks.html: In a large network, data passes through many intermediate devices called switches or nodes. Switching decides how the data travels from sender to receiver.

items.html: A dedicated path is set up between sender and receiver before communication starts, and it stays reserved until the end.
Data flows in order with no waiting at each node.
Example: the old landline telephone call.
Weakness: the path is wasted during silence, and setting it up takes time.
The message is broken into small packets. Each packet carries a header with the source address, the destination address and a sequence number.
Packets travel independently and may take different routes.
At the destination they are reassembled in the correct order using the sequence numbers.
No dedicated path: the lines are shared by many users. This is how the Internet works.

blocks.text: 11.8.2 Detecting errors with a parity bit

blocks.html: Noise on a line can flip a bit from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. A simple check is the even parity bit: the sender adds one extra bit so that the total number of 1s is even. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error has happened.
1011001 has four 1s (already even), so the parity bit is 0. After bit 2 flips, there are three
1s (odd), so the error is caught. A parity bit cannot catch two flipped bits, which is why real networks use stronger checks such as CRC.
The Internet can deliver packets out of order. TCP uses the sequence numbers to put them back in order, and we can do the same with sort (Chapter 5).
The 17-character message makes 4 packets: RESUL , TS OU , T TOD and AY .

items.html: Data communication is the exchange of data between devices. Its components are the sender, receiver, message, medium and protocol.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies (Hz). The data transfer rate is measured in bps, Kbps, Mbps and Gbps. 1 byte = 8 bits.
Simplex = one way. Half-duplex = both ways, one at a time. Full-duplex = both ways together.
Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path. Packet switching splits data into numbered packets that may take different routes and are reassembled at the destination; the Internet uses it.
Guided media: twisted pair (LAN), coaxial (cable TV), optical fibre (fast, long distance, uses light). Unguided media: radio, microwave (line of sight), infrared (very short range), satellite.
Mobile generations: 1G analog voice, 2G digital and SMS, 3G mobile Internet, 4G fast all-IP data, 5G gigabit speeds and very low latency (India, 2022).
Protocols: HTTP and HTTPS (web), FTP (files), SMTP (sending mail), POP3 and IMAP (receiving mail), PPP (point-to-point), TCP/IP (the Internet's core).
A parity bit detects single-bit errors.
